questions.q: Why should a baseline come before any complex model?
options: It sets the bar and shows the lift of your model
why: No law requires it.
Correct: you cannot say a model is good without a bar to beat.
It often wins, but not always, so you must test.
Speed to type is not the reason.

questions.q: Why is a random train/test split wrong for time series?
options: Training rows can come from after test rows, so the model sees the future
why: Speed is not the issue.
Correct: the model can learn from the future and the score is too good.
Seasonality stays in the data.
Memory is not the issue.

questions.q: Which is the best definition of a stationary series?
options: Mean, variance and autocorrelation do not change over time
why: A stationary series still moves around.
Correct: its statistical behaviour is stable over time.
Stationary series can be noisy; white noise is stationary.
A clear trend breaks stationarity.

questions.q: You see a slow decay in the ACF and a trend. What is the usual first step before ARIMA?
why: Dropping data does not fix the trend.
Correct: differencing removes a trend and makes the series closer to stationary.
More lags do not fix a trend.
Metric choice is separate.

questions.q: What happens to MAPE when an actual value is zero?
why: The error is divided by the actual, not multiplied.
Correct: dividing by zero is undefined, so MAPE breaks.
The result is not one.
It breaks exactly because the actual is in the denominator.

questions.q: Actuals are [100, 200, 50] and forecasts are [110, 180, 70]. What is WAPE? (give a decimal, e.g. 0.14)
questions.why: Absolute errors: 10 + 20 + 20 = 50. Sum of actuals: 350. WAPE = 50 / 350 = 0.143.

questions.q: In-sample naive MAE (one step) on the training data is 1.6667. The model's test MAE is 2.0. What is MASE?
questions.why: MASE = test MAE / naive MAE = 2.0 / 1.6667 = 1.2. A value above 1 means worse than the naive method.

questions.q: MASE = 0.8 on the test set. What does it mean?
options: The model's error is 20% lower than the naive in-sample error
The model is worse than naive
why: MASE is not an accuracy percent.
Correct: 0.8 is below 1, so the model beats the naive error by 20%.
Worse than naive would be above 1.
MASE is valid when the naive error is above zero.

questions.q: Pinball loss for quantile q = 0.9: the actual is 100 and the forecast is 90. What is the loss?
questions.why: The forecast is below the actual, so loss = q × (actual − forecast) = 0.9 × 10 = 9.

questions.q: A 90% prediction interval should contain the actual value about how often?
why: 50% is a different interval.
Correct: coverage should match the stated level.
99% would be a wider interval.
Coverage is about calibration, not MAE.

questions.q: Series length 100. First training window 60 days, horizon 10, step 10 (expanding window). How many backtest origins fit?
questions.why: Training ends at day 60, 70, 80, 90. A test window of 10 days must fit, so the last origin is 90 (test is days 91-100). That gives 4 origins.

questions.q: Which is a leakage example?
options: A 7-day rolling mean that includes today's value, used to predict today
A holiday flag known in advance
why: Lag-7 uses the past.
Correct: today's value is not known at prediction time.
Holiday dates are known in advance.
Day of week is known in advance.

questions.q: When does a global model usually beat many local models?
options: When you have one long series
When you have many related series with short histories
why: With one series, a local model is the natural choice.
Correct: a global model learns shared patterns across series.
With no pattern, nothing helps.
Intervals do not decide this.

questions.q: What is the main risk of recursive multi-step forecasting?
options: Errors in early steps feed into later steps and accumulate
why: Memory is not the main risk.
Correct: each forecast becomes an input, so errors can grow.
Recursive models use lags heavily.
Simplicity is not a risk.

questions.q: For intermittent demand (many zeros), which method family is designed for it?
why: Correct: Croston and TSB model demand size and interval separately.
Holt-Winters assumes a smooth series.
Seasonal ARIMA assumes a smooth series too.
DTW compares shapes, not forecasts of sparse demand.

questions.q: What does reconciliation do in hierarchical forecasting?
options: Makes forecasts at different levels add up consistently
why: It does not touch seasonality.
Correct: store forecasts should sum to the region forecast.
It is a post-step, not a model type.
The horizon is unchanged.

questions.q: Which tool is best to flag a sudden jump in the mean of a series?
why: ACF does not locate a level shift.
Correct: CUSUM and similar methods are made for mean shifts.
Seasonal naive is a forecast baseline.
Quantile loss trains intervals.

questions.q: SES with alpha = 0.5, last forecast 100, new actual 120. What is the next forecast?
why: That ignores the new data.
That means alpha = 1.
That is not the formula.

questions.q: What is the newsvendor critical ratio when under-stocking costs 3 and over-stocking costs 1 per unit?
why: That would be 1 / (3 + 1), the over-stock share.
That is for equal costs.
Correct: 3 / (3 + 1) = 0.75, so stock at the 75th percentile.
A ratio of 1 means infinite shortage cost.

questions.q: A model works well in backtest but poorly after launch. Which is the first thing to check?
options: Leakage or a difference between offline and live data
why: Not relevant.
Correct: the usual causes are leakage, late data, and different feature timing.
Layer count is rarely the first cause.
Not relevant.

questions.q: When is a foundation model a good first try?
options: When you have little history per series and want a strong zero-shot baseline to compare
When you need the lowest latency at huge scale
When data is private and cannot leave your network
why: It is a useful tool in some cases.
Correct: zero-shot models help with short history and quick baselines.
Large models are often slow and costly at scale.
Privacy may block API use; self-hosting is a separate choice.

questions.q: Which of these belong in a leakage-free feature pipeline? (choose all)
options: Lags computed with shift(h) for h at least the horizon
Rolling stats computed on data up to t-1
Scaling with mean and std from the full dataset
why: Correct: shifted lags only use the past.
Correct: windows must end before the forecast time.
Wrong: full-data statistics leak the future into training.
Correct: planned promotions are known-future covariates.

questions.q: Which are good signs in a take-home forecasting report? (choose all)
options: A clear README to run the code
why: Correct: a baseline is required.
Wrong: a random split is a classic mistake.
Correct: segment error shows where the model fails.
Correct: reviewers must be able to run your work.
